issues.legal_issue: A consolidation scheme reserving land to generate income for a public body constitutes acquisition by the State and cannot stand where it takes land held within the legal ceiling without satisfying the constitutional protection.
material_facts: The consolidation scheme reserved land to generate income for the village Panchayat.
The income belonged to the Panchayat, which was a State body for constitutional purposes, even though it could be used only for the village community.
The petitioner held land within the applicable ceiling.
issues.conclusion: The reservation for Panchayat income was contrary to the second proviso to Article 31A(1), and the scheme had to be modified accordingly.
issues.legal_principle: Under the second proviso to Article 31A(1), acquisition by the State is distinct from modification or extinguishment of rights where the beneficiary is not the State. A Panchayat is within the meaning of State in Article 12. The Court followed Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab. It also rejected treating Panchayat income as a non-State benefit merely because it must be used for the village community; section 2(bb) of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, defines common purpose to include providing income for the Panchayat for that benefit.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_consolidatio: A person challenges a land-consolidation scheme on constitutional grounds.
predicates.landholding_within_ceiling: The affected landholder's holding is within the legally fixed ceiling.
predicates.scheme_reserves_land_for_public_body_inc: The scheme reserves land so that a public body receives income from it.
predicates.beneficiary_is_state: The public body benefiting from the reservation is part of the State for constitutional purposes.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a consolidation scheme that reserves land within a landholder's ceiling for income benefiting the State, the scheme must be modified to remove that reservation.

issues.legal_issue: Repartition under a consolidation scheme does not complete acquisition before possession changes where management, control, and the holders' rights remain untransferred until then.
material_facts: Repartition under the scheme had been effected before the constitutional protection was introduced.
Possession had not been transferred because of court stay orders.
Under sections 23A and 24 of the Act, management and control vested in the Panchayat, and the holders' rights were modified or extinguished, only when possession changed.
issues.conclusion: Acquisition had not already taken place before the second proviso to Article 31A(1) came into force, so the scheme was not exempt from that proviso on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 23A and 24 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, management and control do not vest in the Panchayat, and the holders' rights are not modified or extinguished, until possession changes. Finalising rights to possession by repartition alone is not acquisition for the second proviso to Article 31A(1). The Court followed Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_consolidatio: A person challenges a land-consolidation scheme on constitutional grounds.
predicates.repartition_completed: The authorities have completed the allocation of land under the consolidation scheme.
predicates.possession_not_transferred_when_constitu: The persons entitled to the newly allocated holdings have not taken possession when the constitutional protection becomes applicable.

issues.definition: If repartition has been completed in a constitutional challenge to a consolidation scheme but possession has not been transferred when the protection applies, acquisition is not complete.

issues.legal_issue: A cultivating tenant whose holding is reduced below the legal ceiling by a State acquisition must receive compensation at no less than market value.
material_facts: The scheme reserved land for the Panchayat, reducing the petitioner's holding below the legal ceiling.
The petitioner was a cultivating landholder affected by the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: In the dissenting opinion, compensation at a rate not below market value was required for the land that reduced the holding below the ceiling.
issues.legal_principle: The dissenting judges interpreted the second proviso to Article 31A(1) to require market-value compensation where State acquisition reduces a cultivating tenant's holding below the ceiling. They relied on the approach set out in their judgment in the companion case, Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab, and rejected indirect advantages from the later use of the land as a substitute for market-value compensation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenges a State acquisition of land on constitutional grounds.
predicates.affected_holder_is_cultivating_tenant: The person whose land is acquired cultivates the affected holding as a tenant.
predicates.acquisition_reduces_holding_below_ceilin: The acquisition leaves the affected holder with less land than the legally fixed ceiling.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a State acquisition that reduces a cultivating tenant's holding below the legal ceiling, market-rate compensation must be paid.
